As we have already suggested, this tale is closely connected with the one before it. “The Tale of the Crimson Archangel” ends with a condition: “If you are Khezr, you too can cross Mount Qâf”—that is, you can reach the Spring of Life. “The Tale of the Western Exile” removes the uncertainty. The spiritual seeker will prove capable of joining Khezr at the Spring of Life; or, more precisely, he will undertake Khezr's quest again, in the first person.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01339

But the setting has changed completely. There is no longer any direct reference to the heroic epic of Iran. As we have just seen, that epic has already found its fulfilment in an epic of mystical gnosis. Now it is the gnostic himself who will live out his own story. He will fulfil the conditions of the threefold unity of the hikâyat, the mystical tale or recital, which we encountered earlier. Everything we learn in the course of the tale shows its hero to be a representative figure of mystical gnosis in Islam.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01340

The title itself is remarkably suggestive. The founding of “Eastern theosophy” is answered by “The Tale of the Western Exile.” The entire “history” of the gnostic is contained in the tension between these two terms. It really is a history, though not history in the ordinary sense of the word—the sense usually invoked when people contrast a Christian feeling for salvation as a historical event with the Greek philosophers' understanding of the world. It is precisely because this opposition is too crude that so many judgments about gnosis miss its true nature entirely. We sometimes hear that the gnostic “flees” the world and therefore goes against “the direction of history.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01341

But such a judgment simply assumes what it needs to prove. To rest content with it is to presume that the very question under dispute has already been settled: what does the “phenomenon of the world” itself mean? Yet it is precisely this question that motivates the challenge voiced by gnosis. The person who feels like a stranger in this world is someone who has awakened to the knowledge that his origin and his ultimate destination lie elsewhere.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01342

To feel entirely “at home” in this world is, for all forms of gnosis, the tragedy itself. Whoever accuses gnosis of fleeing the world would do better to say openly that he, for his part, does not believe in that elsewhere. And whoever accuses it of moving against “the direction of history” deliberately overlooks the gnostic's own “history.” Others claim that gnosis merely adds truths known to the truths believed. Sohrawardî's “Tale of the Exile” is enough to expose the mistake in that way of seeing things.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01343

We have already stressed the three degrees of certainty: knowledge or theoretical certainty ('ilm al-yaqîn); the certainty of an eyewitness ('ayn al-yaqîn); and the certainty of someone who experiences the reality of what he knows because it actually takes place within him (haqq al-yaqîn). It is this third degree that characterizes gnostic truth. That is why the Qur'anic verses, brought by spiritual interpretation to the level of haqq al-yaqîn, will mark the stages of the homeward journey in this tale. A parallel could be drawn here with the spiritual interpretation practised by gnostic traditions outside Islam.
